title: Hash Map: Group Anagrams
oneLiner: Give every word a key that all of its anagrams share, then let a hash map do the grouping in one pass.
keyTakeaway: Grouping by "same up to rearrangement" means finding a canonical form: a value that is identical for every member of a group and different across groups. For anagrams that is the sorted word (or a 26-slot letter count). Use it as a hash map key and each word joins its group in one lookup, instead of being compared against every other word.
explanation:
Given an array of lowercase words, group together the words that are anagrams of each other (the same letters with the same counts, in any order) and return the groups. For ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"] the groups are [eat, tea, ate], [tan, nat], and [bat]. The order of the groups and of the words inside each group doesn't matter; the tests sort both before comparing.

The obvious approach compares every pair of words with an anagram check, which is O(n²) checks. The better question is: what do anagrams have in common that you can compute from one word alone? Sort the letters. "eat", "tea" and "ate" all sort to "aet", and no word outside that group does. That sorted string is a canonical form, and canonical forms make perfect hash map keys.

So: make a map from key to list of words. For each word, compute its key, look it up, and append the word to that list (creating the list the first time the key appears). At the end, the map's values are the groups. Each word costs one sort of its letters, O(L log L) for a word of length L, so the total is O(n · L log L).

If the alphabet is small and fixed, you can skip the sort: count each letter into a 26-slot array and use the counts as the key (joined into a string like "1#0#0#..." in C#, or as a tuple in Python). That is O(L) per word, so O(n · L) total. The separator matters: without one, counts of 1 and 11 can run together and two different words can end up with the same key. Both keys work for this lesson. The same idea (map each item to a canonical key) also groups shifted strings ("abc", "bcd"), isomorphic words, and points on the same line.

The visualization shows the map's entries as each word is added.

visualizationSteps.message: Words: [eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]. The map starts empty. Each cell below will be one entry, shown as key: group.
"eat" sorts to "aet". New key, so start a group: aet: [eat].
"tea" sorts to "aet", which is already in the map. Append it: aet: [eat, tea].
"tan" sorts to "ant". New key, so start a group: ant: [tan].
"ate" sorts to "aet", which is already in the map. Append it: aet: [eat, tea, ate].
"nat" sorts to "ant", which is already in the map. Append it: ant: [tan, nat].
"bat" sorts to "abt". New key, so start a group: abt: [bat].
Done in one pass. The map's values are the 3 groups: [eat, tea, ate], [tan, nat], [bat].

recognitionSignals: "Group", "bucket", or "classify" items that are equivalent under some rearrangement or transformation.
A pairwise "are these two the same kind?" check exists, but comparing every pair would be O(n²).
You can compute something from ONE item alone that is identical for every member of its group.
gotchas: A list or array is not a usable dictionary key in either language: C# compares int[] by reference and Python can't hash a list. Convert to a string (or a tuple in Python).
When you build a count-based key as a string, put a separator between the counts. Without one, different count arrays can produce the same string.
Duplicates are real words too: ["x", "x"] is one group of two, not one group of one.
confusableWith: Hash Maps: Two Sum uses the map to remember values already seen so a later element can find its partner. Here the map is a bucketing tool: the key is computed, and every item lands in exactly one bucket.
Sorting the whole input does not group anagrams, because "ate" and "bat" would sit next to each other. It's each WORD that gets sorted, to build its key.

complexity.note: Each of the n words (length up to L) is sorted to build its key, O(L log L) each. A 26-slot count key instead costs O(L) per word, so O(n · L). The map stores every word plus its key.
